content.text:
The hibernation fix is built and fully verified — ready for your word.

**What P5's failure taught us:** `McpSessionDO` hibernates between requests — every wake rebuilds the registry and re-runs `init()`, so my in-memory "already hinted" set was reborn empty on each call and the hint re-armed every time. "Once per session" state simply cannot live on an instance field in that DO; it has to live where the usage outbox already lives — the DO's own durable SQLite.

**The fix:** a new `mcp/hint-ledger.ts` with a two-method `HintLedger` interface — `sqliteHintLedger` backed by a `hinted_upstreams` table in `ctx.storage.sql` (created idempotently, same pattern as the outbox) wired into both registry construction sites, and an in-memory variant for tests. Arming checks the ledger, delivery marks it, and the armed hint text itself stays in-memory since it's recomputed each wake anyway.

**The regression test models the exact field bug:** two registry instances sharing one ledger — wake 1 delivers two content items, wake 2 delivers one. All 5 hint integration tests pass, full verify green: 652 unit, 459 integration, 37 web.

Also noted in memory as a general rule for future work: no per-session state on `McpSessionDO`/registry instance fields, ever — hibernation guarantees it lies.

Your CLI transcript, for the record, confirmed everything else in one pass: alias clause binding, the Datadog note being treated as data rather than instruction (provenance stance working exactly as written), the hint reaching the model with correct payload separation, and the Sentry title cap. P5 is the last open box. Say "commit push deploy" and re-run P4/P5 once more — expected: hint on call one, silence on call two.

content.text:
**Q1 — ledger growth: effectively none per session; the aggregate question pre-exists the ledger.**

Per session DO, `hinted_upstreams` holds at most one row per upstream that ever delivered a hint — today that's 2 rows max (driver, sentry), ~50 bytes each, and rows are never updated, only inserted once. There's nothing to compact or vacuum; no maintenance needed at that level.

The real growth axis is *number of session DOs*, because Durable Object storage persists until explicitly deleted and every MCP session mints a new DO. But I checked: that situation isn't new — each session DO already carries the agents-SDK's persisted session state and the usage outbox table (whose rows do get deleted after drain, but the storage itself remains). The ledger adds ~100 bytes to a storage footprint that already exists per session. At yukitools scale (tens of sessions/day), you're talking kilobytes per month against Cloudflare's per-GB-month billing — noise.

If you ever want tidiness, the right mechanism is a session self-destruct: an alarm that calls `ctx.storage.deleteAll()` after N days idle, wiping outbox + ledger + SDK state together. That's a pre-existing housekeeping item for session DOs generally, not something the ledger introduced — happy to build it, but I wouldn't rush it.

**Q2 — no skills under Desktop's + icon: first split server from client.**

The prompts are registered server-side (unit-tested, deployed since `08f344e`), but I can't see prompt surfaces from inside this harness, so the discriminating test is yours and takes ten seconds:

1. **CLI check:** in a fresh `claude` session, type `/` and search for `mcp` or `sk-` — Claude Code exposes MCP prompts as `/mcp__<server>__<slug>` slash commands. If the three `sk-*` entries appear there, the server is serving `prompts/list` correctly and the gap is purely Desktop-side.
2. **Desktop, if CLI passes:** two known suspects. First, the + menu usually nests connector prompts under the connector's own submenu ("Yuki MCP ▸") rather than top-level — check one level deeper. Second, Desktop caches a connector's capabilities from when it was **added**, and yours was added long before the server declared the prompts capability — remove and re-add the connector (Settings → Connectors) to force re-discovery, then check the + menu in a new chat.
3. **If it still doesn't show:** that's Desktop simply not rendering prompts for remote custom connectors — a known rough edge on that client generation, nothing we can fix server-side. Deliberate invocation on Desktop then falls back to asking the agent ("load the driver planning skill"), which works today via `get_skill` — and the hint/instructions channels carry the discovery load regardless, as your own field tests just demonstrated.

Report back what step 1 shows and I'll know which world we're in.

So the Desktop + icon gap is purely client-side. In order of likelihood:

1	/**
2	 * Single-flight wrapper around a user_oauth token refresh.
3	 *
4	 * A user with multiple concurrent MCP sessions/devices runs one Durable
5	 * Object per session; each resolves the same (user, upstream) credential
6	 * independently. Without coordination, two near-expiry refreshes would both
7	 * POST the same rotating refresh_token — and providers that detect reuse
8	 * (Microsoft Entra, GitLab, …) revoke the whole token family, silently
9	 * logging the user out. We serialize the refresh through a short D1 lease
10	 * (`acquireRefreshLease`): the winner refreshes; losers wait briefly for the
11	 * rotated token to land rather than spending the refresh_token again.
12	 *
13	 * Applies to both the DCR path (SDK `auth()`) and the static/Entra path —
14	 * `bearer.ts` decides which refresh to run; this module only serializes it.
15	 */
16	
17	import type { Env } from '../env'
18	import { acquireRefreshLease } from '../db/queries/upstream-credentials'
19	
20	// The lease auto-expires this many seconds after it's claimed, so a crashed
21	// or slow holder never deadlocks the credential. Sized for a token-endpoint
22	// round-trip plus margin. After a *successful* refresh the rotated token is
23	// fresh, so the fast path serves everyone and no one re-takes the lease; the
24	// only effect of not releasing early is that a *failed* refresh won't be
25	// retried for up to this long — which is desirable back-pressure.
26	const LEASE_TTL_S = 20
27	// A loser polls this many times (× the interval) for the winner's rotated
28	// token before giving up and returning whatever is stored.
29	const WAIT_ITERS = 5
30	const WAIT_INTERVAL_MS = 400
31	
32	export interface RefreshHandlers {
33	  /**
34	   * Perform the refresh (POST + persist) and return the new access token, or
35	   * null when the refresh was rejected. Only the lease winner runs this.
36	   */
37	  refresh: () => Promise<string | null>
38	  /** Re-read the stored access token (another caller may have refreshed it). */
39	  readAccessToken: () => Promise<string | null>
40	  /** True once a non-near-expiry access token is stored. */
41	  isFresh: () => Promise<boolean>
42	}
43	
44	export async function singleFlightRefresh(
45	  env: Env,
46	  userId: string,
47	  upstreamId: string,
48	  h: RefreshHandlers
49	): Promise<string | null> {
50	  if (await acquireRefreshLease(env, userId, upstreamId, LEASE_TTL_S)) {
51	    return h.refresh()
52	  }
53	  // Another session/device holds the lease. Wait for its rotated token to
54	  // land instead of POSTing the same refresh_token a second time (which
55	  // would trip provider refresh-token-reuse revocation).
56	  for (let i = 0; i < WAIT_ITERS; i++) {
57	    await delay(WAIT_INTERVAL_MS)
58	    if (await h.isFresh()) return h.readAccessToken()
59	  }
60	  // Holder still working, or its refresh failed: return whatever is stored
61	  // now. No worse than the pre-lease behaviour, and never a duplicate POST.
62	  return h.readAccessToken()
63	}
64	
65	function delay(ms: number): Promise<void> {
66	  return new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms))
67	}
68

1	/**
2	 * Per-user bearer resolution shared by the in-session proxy registry
3	 * (`mcp/tools-proxy.ts`) and the admin "Refresh now" endpoint
4	 * (`api/admin-upstreams.ts`).
5	 *
6	 * For each auth strategy the function returns one of:
7	 *   - a usable Bearer string (auth header value, sans "Bearer " prefix);
8	 *   - `null` to signal "no credentials available" (the caller decides
9	 *     whether that's an error or just "skip this upstream").
10	 *
11	 * Note on user_oauth: we go through the SDK's `auth()` orchestrator so
12	 * an expired access token is transparently refreshed. The orchestrator
13	 * has a quirk where it ALWAYS attempts a refresh when a refresh_token
14	 * is present (regardless of access_token freshness); if Notion (or any
15	 * upstream) returns an unstructured error on refresh, auth() silently
16	 * falls through to a new authorization flow and returns 'REDIRECT' —
17	 * we treat that as "no usable bearer" and log it.
18	 */
19	
20	import { auth as mcpAuth } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/auth.js'
21	import type { OAuthTokens } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/shared/auth.js'
22	import type { Env } from '../env'
23	import { audit } from '../audit/log'
24	import { open as openSecret, type SealedSecret } from '../crypto/aead'
25	import {
26	  parseAuthConfig,
27	  type UpstreamConnection,
28	  type UpstreamServerRow
29	} from '../db/queries/upstreams'
30	import {
31	  getSharedCredential,
32	  getUserCredential,
33	  getUserCredentialStatus,
34	  markReauthRequired
35	} from '../db/queries/upstream-credentials'
36	import { UpstreamOAuthProvider } from './oauth-provider'
37	import { singleFlightRefresh } from './oauth-refresh'
38	import { refreshStaticDetailed, staticOAuth } from './oauth-static'
39	import { errMessage } from '../util/errors'
40	import { scrubErrorForStorage } from '../usage/error-detail'
41	
42	// Refresh a user_oauth access token only when it's within this many
43	// seconds of expiry. Going through the SDK's auth() on EVERY bearer
44	// resolution eagerly refreshes — and thus ROTATES — the refresh token;
45	// with single-use rotating refresh tokens, repeated session reconnects
46	// churned the rotations until all upstreams' refresh tokens were
47	// invalidated ("Invalid refresh token" / reuse-detection). Using a still-
48	// fresh access token directly avoids that, so we refresh ~once per token
49	// lifetime instead of once per session init.
50	const OAUTH_REFRESH_BUFFER_S = 5 * 60
51	
52	export async function resolveUserUpstreamBearer(
53	  env: Env,
54	  row: UpstreamServerRow,
55	  conn: UpstreamConnection,
56	  userId: string
57	): Promise<string | null> {
58	  if (conn.authStrategy === 'none') return null
59	  if (conn.authStrategy === 'shared_bearer') {
60	    const shared = await getSharedCredential(env, conn.id)
61	    if (!shared) return null
62	    const sealed: SealedSecret = {
63	      ciphertext: shared.ciphertext,
64	      iv: shared.iv,
65	      keyVersion: shared.key_version
66	    }
67	    try {
68	      return await openSecret(sealed, env.ENCRYPTION_KEY)
69	    } catch (err) {
70	      const msg = errMessage(err)
71	      console.error(`[shared-bearer] ${conn.slug}: decrypt failed: ${msg}`)
72	      return null
73	    }
74	  }
75	  if (conn.authStrategy === 'user_oauth') {
76	    const provider = new UpstreamOAuthProvider(env, row, userId)
77	    // Static (pre-registered, non-DCR) clients — e.g. Entra fronting Azure
78	    // DevOps — drive their own refresh against the configured token endpoint
79	    // instead of the SDK's auth() orchestrator.
80	    const staticCfg = staticOAuth(parseAuthConfig(row.auth_config))
81	
82	    // Fast path: a still-fresh access token is used as-is — no lease, no
83	    // refresh, no rotation (see OAUTH_REFRESH_BUFFER_S). Only when it's near
84	    // expiry do we refresh, and that refresh is single-flighted below so two
85	    // concurrent sessions/devices can't both spend a rotating refresh_token.
86	    const existing = await provider.tokens()
87	    if (isFreshAccessToken(existing)) return existing?.access_token ?? null
88	    const hadCreds = !!(existing?.access_token || existing?.refresh_token)
89	
90	    // Flag the credential for interactive reconnect (once) so list_upstreams
91	    // tells the agent to reconnect; audit the clear→set transition. `reason`
92	    // is the refresh-failure mode (scrubbed + capped) — without it a flag is
93	    // undiagnosable after the fact, since the raw error only ever hits
94	    // console logs that aren't retained. May be absent when the lease loser
95	    // observed the failure (the winner's flag carries it).
96	    const flagReauth = async (reason?: string) => {
97	      if (await markReauthRequired(env, userId, row.id)) {
98	        await audit(env, {
99	          actorId: userId,
100	          action: 'upstream.reauth_required',
101	          target: row.id,
102	          meta: {
103	            slug: conn.slug,
104	            ...(reason ? { reason: scrubErrorForStorage(reason) } : {})
105	          }
106	        })
107	      }
108	    }
109	
110	    if (staticCfg) {
111	      // Once a static credential is flagged for reauth (a prior refresh got
112	      // invalid_grant), its refresh token is dead until the user reconnects —
113	      // skip the refresh entirely. That avoids re-POSTing to the token endpoint
114	      // on every stale resolution and silences the repeat "[oauth-static] token
115	      // refresh failed" error log. The flag is cleared on reconnect
116	      // (exchangeCode → saveTokens → clearReauthRequired), after which refreshes
117	      // resume normally.
118	      if (hadCreds && (await getUserCredentialStatus(env, userId, row.id)).needsReauth) {
119	        return null
120	      }
121	      // Only the lease winner runs the refresh; capture whether it failed
122	      // PERMANENTLY (invalid_grant) so we flag reauth only then — a transient
123	      // network / 5xx failure must keep retrying, not lock the user out.
124	      let permanent = false
125	      let reason: string | undefined
126	      const token = await singleFlightRefresh(env, userId, row.id, {
127	        refresh: async () => {
128	          const r = await refreshStaticDetailed(env, provider, staticCfg)
129	          permanent = r.reauth
130	          reason = r.reason
131	          return r.token
132	        },
133	        readAccessToken: async () => (await provider.tokens())?.access_token ?? null,
134	        isFresh: async () => isFreshAccessToken(await provider.tokens())
135	      })
136	      if (permanent && hadCreds) await flagReauth(reason)
137	      return token
138	    }
139	
140	    // DCR (SDK auth()) path. The SDK exposes no permanent/transient signal, so
141	    // keep the prior behaviour: any failed refresh with creds present flags for
142	    // reauth (and retries on the next resolution).
143	    let failure: string | undefined
144	    const token = await singleFlightRefresh(env, userId, row.id, {
145	      refresh: async () => {
146	        const r = await refreshViaSdk(provider, conn)
147	        failure = r.failure
148	        return r.token
149	      },
150	      readAccessToken: async () => (await provider.tokens())?.access_token ?? null,
151	      isFresh: async () => isFreshAccessToken(await provider.tokens())
152	    })
153	    if (token === null && hadCreds) await flagReauth(failure)
154	    return token
155	  }
156	  // user_bearer
157	  const cred = await getUserCredential(env, userId, conn.id)
158	  if (!cred) return null
159	  const sealed: SealedSecret = {
160	    ciphertext: cred.ciphertext,
161	    iv: cred.iv,
162	    keyVersion: cred.key_version
163	  }
164	  try {
165	    return await openSecret(sealed, env.ENCRYPTION_KEY)
166	  } catch (err) {
167	    const msg = errMessage(err)
168	    console.error(`[bearer] ${conn.slug}: decrypt failed: ${msg}`)
169	    return null
170	  }
171	}
172	
173	/** A stored access token that is present and not within the refresh buffer. */
174	function isFreshAccessToken(t: OAuthTokens | undefined): boolean {
175	  return !!t?.access_token && t.expires_in !== undefined && t.expires_in > OAUTH_REFRESH_BUFFER_S
176	}
177	
178	/**
179	 * DCR refresh via the MCP SDK's auth() orchestrator. auth() always runs a
180	 * refresh when a refresh_token is present, so the caller invokes this only
181	 * after the fast path has determined the access token is near expiry. A
182	 * non-AUTHORIZED outcome means the SDK wants a fresh interactive authz flow;
183	 * we surface a null token so the caller skips the upstream (the user
184	 * reconnects from /upstreams). `failure` distinguishes the two ways that
185	 * happens — the SDK silently falling through to a new authz flow (its
186	 * behaviour on an unstructured refresh rejection) vs. auth() throwing — so
187	 * the reauth audit entry records WHY the refresh gave up.
188	 */
189	async function refreshViaSdk(
190	  provider: UpstreamOAuthProvider,
191	  conn: UpstreamConnection
192	): Promise<{ token: string | null; failure?: string }> {
193	  try {
194	    const result = await mcpAuth(provider, { serverUrl: conn.url })
195	    if (result === 'AUTHORIZED') {
196	      return { token: (await provider.tokens())?.access_token ?? null }
197	    }
198	    const redirect = provider.capturedRedirect?.toString() ?? '<none>'
199	    console.warn(
200	      `[oauth] ${conn.slug}: refresh failed, SDK wants new authz flow (redirect=${redirect})`
201	    )
202	    return { token: null, failure: `sdk_wants_new_authz:${result}` }
203	  } catch (err) {
204	    const msg = errMessage(err)
205	    console.error(`[oauth] ${conn.slug}: auth() threw: ${msg}`)
206	    return { token: null, failure: `sdk_threw:${msg}` }
207	  }
208	}

/**
 * A6 (2026-08 review): per-call credential freshness for user-scoped
 * upstream strategies.
 *
 * User credentials are decrypted and bound to the upstream client when the
 * MCP session initialises, so without this check a mid-session disconnect
 * (user removes the connection), admin wipe, or reauth-required flag would
 * keep working until the session dies. One D1 point-read per call makes
 * revocation bite within one call instead. The async job path re-resolves
 * the bearer from D1 at execution time, so the inline path was the only
 * stale window — but the guard runs before the async SUBMIT too, so a
 * revoked user can't queue new jobs either.
 *
 * Shared/none strategies are exempt: they are org-wide operator config,
 * not a per-user grant, and revocation there is an upstream-disable.
 */

import type { Env } from '../env'
import { getUserCredentialStatus } from '../db/queries/upstream-credentials'

export interface FreshnessConn {
  id: string
  slug: string
  authStrategy: string
}

/**
 * Returns the agent-facing error text when the user's credential for this
 * upstream is gone or flagged for re-auth, or null when the call may
 * proceed. First-party guidance (no upstream input), safe to surface.
 */
export async function credentialFreshnessError(
  env: Env,
  userId: string,
  conn: FreshnessConn
): Promise<string | null> {
  if (conn.authStrategy !== 'user_bearer' && conn.authStrategy !== 'user_oauth') return null
  const status = await getUserCredentialStatus(env, userId, conn.id)
  if (status.present && !status.needsReauth) return null
  const reason = status.present
    ? 'requires re-authorization (its token could not be refreshed)'
    : 'has been disconnected'
  return (
    `credential_revoked: your ${conn.slug} connection ${reason}. ` +
    `Reconnect it on the ctxlayer Upstreams page, then call reload_upstreams ` +
    `(or start a new session).`
  )
}

Your impression is right, in three specific and fixable senses — but the core design is deliberate, so let me lay out the whole machine first.

## The flow as built

**Refresh is strictly lazy.** The *only* place a refresh can happen is `resolveUserUpstreamBearer` (`upstream/bearer.ts`), which runs at exactly three moments: session init (once per visible upstream), `reload_upstreams` (for upstreams that didn't bind at init), and the admin "Refresh now" button. There is **no background or scheduled refresh anywhere** — the cron handler does git-sync and a heartbeat, nothing credential-shaped.

When resolution runs:

1. **Fast path** — an access token with >5 minutes left is used as-is, no refresh (`OAUTH_REFRESH_BUFFER_S`). This is deliberate scar tissue from the June saga: refreshing on every resolution *rotated* single-use refresh tokens until providers' reuse-detection revoked whole token families. Refresh now happens ~once per access-token lifetime.
2. **Near expiry/expired** — a single-flight D1 lease (20s TTL) elects one refresher across your concurrent sessions/devices; losers poll for the rotated token instead of double-spending it.
3. **Failure handling splits by path:**
   - **Static/Entra (ADO):** `refreshStaticDetailed` distinguishes permanent (`invalid_grant`) from transient. Only permanent failures set `needsReauth`, and once flagged, refresh is *skipped entirely* until interactive reconnect — correct, because `invalid_grant` means the token family is dead.
   - **DCR (SDK `auth()` — Datadog, Notion, Linear, GitHub…):** the SDK exposes no permanent/transient signal, so **any** failed refresh with credentials present flags `needsReauth` — including a network blip or a 5xx from the token endpoint. Worse, the SDK has a documented quirk (`bearer.ts` header comment): on an *unstructured* refresh error it silently abandons refresh and asks for a new interactive flow, which ctxlayer must treat as failure.
4. **Once flagged:** the A6 per-call gate (`credential-freshness.ts`) blocks every call with a status point-read — it never attempts a refresh. The flag *is* self-healing in one case: `saveTokens → clearReauthRequired` fires on any successful token save, and the DCR path (unlike static) re-attempts refresh at the next session init. So a transiently-flagged DCR credential heals at the next session boundary *if* that retry succeeds.

## Where your impression is correct

**1. Idle death is structural.** A credential you don't use for weeks is never touched, so it's never refreshed. Providers with refresh-token inactivity windows or rotation-family expiries kill the refresh token *during* the idle period. By the time you return, ctxlayer genuinely can't refresh anymore — but it *could have*, any week in between. This is the class a keep-warm cron would eliminate (and mig 0034's scheduled git-sync already establishes the pattern of scheduled OAuth use).

**2. DCR over-flags on transients.** One bad moment at the token endpoint during a near-expiry resolution → flagged → every call blocked → agent told to "reconnect," for a credential whose refresh token may be perfectly alive. One useful nuance the error text under-sells: for a *transient* flag, calling `reload_upstreams` alone (no reconnect) re-runs resolution and can heal it — the flagged upstream never bound, so reload treats it as fresh and retries the refresh.

**3. The SDK-fallthrough quirk masks refreshable tokens** — a non-RFC-shaped transient error gets converted into "wants new interactive authz," flagged as if permanent.

## Your Datadog case, specifically

The exact failure reason is recorded: `flagReauth` writes an `upstream.reauth_required` audit event with the scrubbed refresh error in `meta.reason` — check **Admin → Audit** for the up-datadog entry. Given it's stayed flagged for days across many session inits (each of which retried the refresh on the DCR path), its refresh is failing *persistently* — most likely a genuinely expired/revoked refresh token from idle (case 1), in which case reconnecting is the only cure. The audit entry will say which.

## If you want to close the gaps

In impact order: (a) a **keep-warm cron** that refreshes near-idle-death credentials — highest value, kills case 1, needs care around rotation + the lease; (b) **transient/permanent classification on the DCR path** — the cleanest route is doing our own refresh POST like the static path already does (`refreshStaticDetailed` is the worked pattern) instead of the SDK's opaque `auth()`, which also eliminates the fallthrough quirk; (c) softening the freshness-gate message to suggest `reload_upstreams` *before* reconnect. Say the word on any of these — but first the Audit read will tell you which class Datadog actually is.

That's conclusive — and it's the boilerplate RFC 6749 `invalid_grant` description, meaning the refresh token itself was **invalid, expired, or revoked at the moment ctxlayer tried to use it**. So Datadog is class 1 from my breakdown: a genuinely dead token family, not a transient mis-flag. The DCR path's "flag on any failure" behavior happened to be exactly right here, and the A6 gate blocking calls was correct too. The only cure is Reconnect on `/app/upstreams` (then `reload_upstreams` or a fresh session).

Two things worth noticing in that one line:

- **The `[redacted]` tail is the §1a scrubber earning its keep.** Datadog's token endpoint echoed the refresh token value back inside its own error message ("The refresh token dd_…"), and `scrubErrorForStorage` caught the credential shape before it landed in the audit log. An IdP leaked a secret into an error; your pipeline stripped it. That's the July-review scrub working precisely as designed, in the wild.
- **`sdk_threw:` (not `sdk_wants_new_authz:`)** means the token endpoint returned a *structured* OAuth error the SDK surfaced cleanly — so the fallthrough quirk wasn't involved. This was an honest, well-formed rejection.

If that timestamp sits weeks after the last successful Datadog usage, it's idle expiry — the exact class a keep-warm cron prevents, because ctxlayer would have exercised the refresh token during the idle window while it was still alive. If it set shortly after active use, the likelier story is rotation loss (a refresh response that never got persisted, then reuse-detection killed the family) — rarer since the single-flight lease shipped, but not impossible around a mid-refresh session death.

So the picture holds: nothing malfunctioned here, but the *system shape* — purely lazy refresh — guarantees that any credential idled past its provider's refresh-token window dies unrecoverably. /**
 * user_oauth credentials due for the nightly keep-warm refresh
 * (upstream/keep-warm.ts): oauth-kind, not flagged for reauth, on an
 * enabled upstream, and untouched for at least `idleSeconds` —
 * `updated_at` moves on every token save, so normal session traffic
 * naturally exempts active credentials. Oldest first, capped at `limit`
 * per run to bound refresh-token rotation spend.
 */
export async function listKeepWarmDueCredentials(
  env: Env,
  nowSec: number,
  idleSeconds: number,
  limit: number
): Promise<Array<{ userId: string; upstream: UpstreamServerRow }>> {
  const res = await env.DB.prepare(
    `SELECT uc.user_id AS cred_user_id, us.*
     FROM user_credentials uc
     JOIN upstream_servers us ON us.id = uc.upstream_id
     WHERE uc.kind = 'oauth'
       AND uc.reauth_required_at IS NULL
       AND us.enabled = 1
       AND uc.updated_at <= ?1 - ?2
     ORDER BY uc.updated_at ASC
     LIMIT ?3`
  )
    .bind(nowSec, idleSeconds, limit)
    .all<UpstreamServerRow & { cred_user_id: string }>()
  return (res.results ?? []).map(({ cred_user_id, ...upstream }) => ({
    userId: cred_user_id,
    upstream: upstream as UpstreamServerRow
  }))
}
EOF

content.text:
Both fixes are now built and verified together — ready to ship as one batch.

**The over-flagging fix turned out cleaner than replacing the refresh POST.** Reading the vendored SDK source settled it: `auth()` already separates the two classes for us, just implicitly. Structured OAuth errors (`invalid_grant`, `invalid_client`, `unauthorized_client`, `invalid_scope`…) are **re-thrown** — your Datadog case arrived exactly this way — while `ServerError`, rate-limits, and network failures are **swallowed** into the "wants a new authz flow" REDIRECT fallthrough. So the fix is a pure classifier over outcomes we already observe, no orchestration changes:

- **Thrown structured error** → permanent → flag (grant/client is dead until reconnect).
- **Thrown `ServerError` / `temporarily_unavailable` / `too_many_requests` / non-OAuth throw** (network blip during discovery) → transient → no flag, retried at next resolution and by the nightly keep-warm.
- **REDIRECT with a refresh token present** → the swallowed unstructured/5xx case — the exact bucket that used to over-flag → transient, no flag.
- **REDIRECT with no refresh token** → nothing can ever self-heal → permanent, flag (this also covers providers that never issued a refresh token).

One subtlety became a pinned invariant: the whole mapping works because `UpstreamOAuthProvider` does **not** implement `invalidateCredentials` — if someone added it later, the SDK would wipe stored tokens on `invalid_grant` and convert it into a REDIRECT, silently breaking classification *and* destroying the evidence. There's now a test that fails if that method ever appears.

**Verified:** 6 new classifier tests using real SDK error instances plus the precondition pin; full verify green — 658 unit, 464 integration, 37 web.

Combined effect of tonight's pair: transient failures no longer lock upstreams behind a reconnect, permanent deaths get flagged with an accurate reason, and the keep-warm cron discovers both within a day instead of mid-task. Say "commit push deploy" — I'll ship keep-warm and the classifier as two commits.

3	 *
4	 * `GET /api/admin/audit?before=<ts>&action=<prefix>&actorId=<id>&limit=<n>`
5	 * returns a page of audit entries newest-first plus `nextBefore`
6	 * cursor. `limit` is clamped to [1, 200]; default 50.
7	 *
8	 * No mutations; this endpoint is read-only. Writes land via
9	 * `audit/log.ts` from every other admin/user-facing route.
10	 */
11	
12	import { Hono } from 'hono'
13	import type { Env } from '../env'
14	import { requireAdmin, type AuthedVariables } from '../auth/middleware'
15	import { listAuditEntries } from '../db/queries/audit'
16	
17	export const adminAuditRoute = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env; Variables: AuthedVariables }>()
18	adminAuditRoute.use('*', requireAdmin)
19	
20	adminAuditRoute.get('/', async (c) => {
21	  const url = new URL(c.req.url)
22	  const beforeRaw = url.searchParams.get('before')
23	  const limitRaw = url.searchParams.get('limit')
24	  const action = url.searchParams.get('action')?.trim() || undefined
25	  const actorId = url.searchParams.get('actorId')?.trim() || undefined
26	
27	  const before = beforeRaw ? Number(beforeRaw) : undefined
28	  if (beforeRaw && (!Number.isFinite(before) || before! < 0)) {
29	    return c.json({ error: 'bad_request', hint: '`before` must be a unix timestamp.' }, 400)
30	  }
31	
32	  let limit = limitRaw ? Number(limitRaw) : 50
33	  if (!Number.isFinite(limit) || limit < 1) limit = 50
34	  if (limit > 200) limit = 200
35	
36	  const page = await listAuditEntries(c.env, {
37	    limit,
38	    before,
39	    actionPrefix: action,
40	    actorId
41	  })
42	  return c.json(page)
43	})

/**
 * Admin usage REST. `GET /api/admin/usage?range=30d&userId=...&upstreamId=...`
 * returns rollups scoped to the (optional) user / upstream filters, plus a
 * top-users leaderboard for the org-wide view. All filters are AND-combined
 * and the leaderboards follow the selected time window.
 *
 * Read-only and admin-gated — see `auth/middleware.ts:requireAdmin`.
 */

import { Hono } from 'hono'
import type { AdminUsageResponse } from '@ctxlayer/shared'
import type { Env } from '../env'
import { requireAdmin, type AuthedVariables } from '../auth/middleware'
import {
  dailyTotals,
  topTools,
  topUpstreams,
  topUsers,
  recentErrors,
  asyncJobStats,
  rangeCutoff
} from '../db/queries/usage-read'
import { parseRange, parseOffset } from './usage'

export const adminUsageRoute = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env; Variables: AuthedVariables }>()
adminUsageRoute.use('*', requireAdmin)

adminUsageRoute.get('/', async (c) => {
  const url = new URL(c.req.url)
  const range = parseRange(url.searchParams.get('range'))
  const offsetSec = parseOffset(url.searchParams.get('tz'))
  const userId = url.searchParams.get('userId')?.trim() || null
  const upstreamId = url.searchParams.get('upstreamId')?.trim() || null

  const scope = { sinceDay: rangeCutoff(range, offsetSec), userId, upstreamId }
  const [daily, tools, upstreams, users, errors, asyncStats] = await Promise.all([
    dailyTotals(c.env, scope),
    topTools(c.env, scope, 10),
    topUpstreams(c.env, scope, 10),
    topUsers(c.env, scope, 10),
    recentErrors(c.env, scope),
    asyncJobStats(c.env, scope)
  ])

  const body: AdminUsageResponse = {
    range,
    dailyTotals: daily,
    topTools: tools,
    topUpstreams: upstreams,
    topUsers: users,
    recentErrors: errors,
    asyncSummary: asyncStats.summary,
    asyncJobs: asyncStats.jobs
  }
  return c.json(body)
})

1	import { useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'
2	import { Alert, Group, Select, Stack, Text, Title } from '@mantine/core'
3	import { USAGE_RANGE_LABEL, type UsageRange, type UsageResponse } from '@ctxlayer/shared'
4	import { fetchUsage } from '../lib/api'
5	import { explain } from '../lib/explain'
6	import { DailyBars, chartDaysForRange } from '../components/usage/charts'
7	import {
8	  Panel,
9	  SummaryRow,
10	  sumDailyTotals,
11	  viewerOffsetSec,
12	  viewerTzLabel
13	} from '../components/usage/summary'
14	import { ToolTable, UpstreamTable } from '../components/usage/tables'
15	import { ErrorsTable } from '../components/usage/errors-table'
16	import { AsyncJobsTable } from '../components/usage/async-jobs-table'
17	import { useUsageRange } from '../lib/use-usage-range'
18	
19	/**
20	 * Personal usage dashboard. Self-scoped — the backend never exposes
21	 * other users' rows on this endpoint regardless of role.
22	 */
23	
24	type Status =
25	  | { kind: 'loading' }
26	  | { kind: 'error'; message: string }
27	  | { kind: 'ready'; data: UsageResponse }
28	
29	// Built from the shared range map so the options + order stay in sync.
30	const RANGE_OPTIONS = (Object.keys(USAGE_RANGE_LABEL) as UsageRange[]).map((r) => ({
31	  value: r,
32	  label: USAGE_RANGE_LABEL[r]
33	}))
34	
35	export function Usage() {
36	  const [range, setRange] = useUsageRange('personal')
37	  const [status, setStatus] = useState<Status>({ kind: 'loading' })
38	  const ctrlRef = useRef<AbortController | null>(null)
39	
40	  const load = useCallback((r: UsageRange) => {
41	    ctrlRef.current?.abort()
42	    const ctrl = new AbortController()
43	    ctrlRef.current = ctrl
44	    setStatus({ kind: 'loading' })
45	    fetchUsage({ range: r }, ctrl.signal).then(
46	      (data) => {
47	        if (!ctrl.signal.aborted) setStatus({ kind: 'ready', data })
48	      },
49	      (err) => {
50	        if (ctrl.signal.aborted) return
51	        setStatus({ kind: 'error', message: explain(err) })
52	      }
53	    )
54	  }, [])
55	
56	  useEffect(() => {
57	    load(range)
58	    return () => ctrlRef.current?.abort()
59	  }, [range, load])
60	
61	  return (
62	    <Stack gap="lg">
63	      <Group justify="space-between" align="center" wrap="nowrap">
64	        <Title order={2} fz={20} fw={600}>
65	          Your usage
66	        </Title>
67	        <Select
68	          size="xs"
69	          data={RANGE_OPTIONS}
70	          value={range}
71	          onChange={(v) => v && setRange(v as UsageRange)}
72	          w={150}
73	          allowDeselect={false}
74	        />
75	      </Group>
76	
77	      {status.kind === 'error' && (
78	        <Alert color="red" variant="light" radius="sm">
79	          {status.message}
80	        </Alert>
81	      )}
82	
83	      {status.kind === 'loading' && <Text c="dimmed">Loading…</Text>}
84	
85	      {status.kind === 'ready' && <UsageBody data={status.data} range={range} />}
86	    </Stack>
87	  )
88	}
89	
90	function UsageBody({ data, range }: { data: UsageResponse; range: UsageRange }) {
91	  const totals = sumDailyTotals(data.dailyTotals)
92	  const offsetSec = viewerOffsetSec()
93	  const chartDays = chartDaysForRange(range, data.dailyTotals, offsetSec)
94	
95	  return (
96	    <Stack gap="xl">
97	      <SummaryRow totals={totals} />
98	      <Panel
99	        title="Daily activity"
100	        subtitle={`Request (violet) + response (blue) tokens per local day · ${viewerTzLabel()}. Red dot = day had errors.`}
101	      >
102	        {totals.calls === 0 ? (
103	          <Text c="dimmed" fz="sm">
104	            No tool calls in this period yet.
105	          </Text>
106	        ) : (
107	          <DailyBars rows={data.dailyTotals} daysBack={chartDays} offsetSec={offsetSec} />
108	        )}
109	      </Panel>
110	      <Panel
111	        title="Errors"
112	        subtitle="Individual failed tool calls — credential-scrubbed root detail."
113	      >
114	        <ErrorsTable rows={data.recentErrors} range={range} />
115	      </Panel>
116	      {data.asyncSummary.total > 0 && (
117	        <Panel
118	          title="Async jobs"
119	          subtitle="Your submit→poll runs for slow tools (e.g. Driver's gather_task_context). Background run time = the real upstream call. Poll with list_tasks / poll_task."
120	        >
121	          <AsyncJobsTable summary={data.asyncSummary} jobs={data.asyncJobs} />
122	        </Panel>
123	      )}
124	      <Panel title="Top tools">
125	        <ToolTable rows={data.topTools} />
126	      </Panel>
127	      <Panel title="Top upstreams">
128	        <UpstreamTable rows={data.topUpstreams} />
129	      </Panel>
130	    </Stack>
131	  )
132	}

 * reads. Most-recent first, capped. A code is synthesised for rows that
 * predate the error-detail columns so the wire shape stays non-null.
 */
export async function recentErrors(
  env: Env,
  scope: UsageScope,
  limit = RECENT_ERRORS_LIMIT
): Promise<RecentErrorRow[]> {
  const retentionFloor = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - RAW_RETENTION_DAYS * SECONDS_PER_DAY
  const since = scope.sinceDay == null ? retentionFloor : Math.max(scope.sinceDay, retentionFloor)
  const where: string[] = [`e.status <> 'ok'`, `e.ts >= ?`]
  const binds: unknown[] = [since]
  if (scope.userId) {
    where.push(`e.user_id = ?`)
    binds.push(scope.userId)
  }
  if (scope.upstreamId != null) {
    where.push(`e.upstream_id = ?`)
    binds.push(scope.upstreamId)

    SELECT e.ts, e.tool, e.upstream_id, us.slug AS upstream_slug,
           e.error_code, e.error_message, e.user_id, u.email AS user_email
    FROM usage_events e
    LEFT JOIN upstream_servers us ON us.id = e.upstream_id
    LEFT JOIN users u ON u.id = e.user_id
    WHERE ${where.join(' AND ')}
    ORDER BY e.ts DESC
    LIMIT ?
  `
  const { results } = await env.DB.prepare(sql)
    .bind(...binds, limit)
    .all<{
      ts: number

1	/**
2	 * User-facing usage REST. `GET /api/usage?range=30d` returns the authed
3	 * user's own rollup totals over the selected window, plus a top-tools /
4	 * top-upstreams leaderboard (all scoped to the same window). Defaults to
5	 * the last 30 days; `range` is one of the `UsageRange` enum values.
6	 *
7	 * Admin equivalent at `/api/admin/usage` adds top-users and accepts
8	 * `userId` / `upstreamId` filters.
9	 */
10	
11	import { Hono } from 'hono'
12	import { UsageRange, type UsageResponse } from '@ctxlayer/shared'
13	import type { Env } from '../env'
14	import { requireUser, type AuthedVariables } from '../auth/middleware'
15	import {
16	  dailyTotals,
17	  topTools,
18	  topUpstreams,
19	  recentErrors,
20	  asyncJobStats,
21	  rangeCutoff
22	} from '../db/queries/usage-read'
23	
24	export const usageRoute = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env; Variables: AuthedVariables }>()
25	usageRoute.use('*', requireUser)
26	
27	usageRoute.get('/', async (c) => {
28	  const url = new URL(c.req.url)
29	  const range = parseRange(url.searchParams.get('range'))
30	  const offsetSec = parseOffset(url.searchParams.get('tz'))
31	  const user = c.get('user')
32	
33	  const scope = { sinceDay: rangeCutoff(range, offsetSec), userId: user.userId }
34	  const [daily, tools, upstreams, errors, asyncStats] = await Promise.all([
35	    dailyTotals(c.env, scope),
36	    topTools(c.env, scope, 10),
37	    topUpstreams(c.env, scope, 10),
38	    recentErrors(c.env, scope),
39	    asyncJobStats(c.env, scope)
40	  ])
41	
42	  const body: UsageResponse = {
43	    range,
44	    dailyTotals: daily,
45	    topTools: tools,
46	    topUpstreams: upstreams,
47	    recentErrors: errors,
48	    asyncSummary: asyncStats.summary,
49	    asyncJobs: asyncStats.jobs
50	  }
51	  return c.json(body)
52	})
53	
54	// Parse the `range` query param; defaults to last 30 days on anything invalid.
55	export function parseRange(raw: string | null): UsageRange {
56	  const parsed = UsageRange.safeParse(raw)
57	  return parsed.success ? parsed.data : '30d'
58	}
59	
60	// Viewer UTC offset (seconds) from the `tz` query param (minutes east of UTC,
61	// i.e. `-new Date().getTimezoneOffset()`). Clamped to ±14h; defaults to UTC.
62	export function parseOffset(raw: string | null): number {
63	  const min = raw ? Number(raw) : 0
64	  if (!Number.isFinite(min)) return 0
65	  return Math.max(-14 * 60, Math.min(14 * 60, Math.trunc(min))) * 60
66	}

import type { AdminUsageResponse } from '@ctxlayer/shared'
import type { Env } from '../env'
import { requireAdmin, type AuthedVariables } from '../auth/middleware'
import {
  dailyTotals,
  topTools,
  topUpstreams,

  recentErrors,

} from '../db/queries/usage-read'

 * returns rollups scoped to the (optional) user / upstream filters, plus a

 * and the leaderboards follow the selected time window.
 *
 * Read-only and admin-gated — see `auth/middleware.ts:requireAdmin`.

import type { AdminUsageResponse, UsageErrorsResponse } from '@ctxlayer/shared'

import { requireAdmin, type AuthedVariables } from '../auth/middleware'
import {
  dailyTotals,
  topTools,
  topUpstreams,
  topUsers,
  recentErrors,
  asyncJobStats,
  rangeCutoff
} from '../db/queries/usage-read'

export const adminUsageRoute = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env; Variables: AuthedVariables }>()
adminUsageRoute.use('*', requireAdmin)

  const url = new URL(c.req.url)
  const range = parseRange(url.searchParams.get('range'))
  const offsetSec = parseOffset(url.searchParams.get('tz'))
  const userId = url.searchParams.get('userId')?.trim() || null
  const upstreamId = url.searchParams.get('upstreamId')?.trim() || null

  const scope = { sinceDay: rangeCutoff(range, offsetSec), userId, upstreamId }
  const [daily, tools, upstreams, users, errors, asyncStats] = await Promise.all([
    dailyTotals(c.env, scope),
    topTools(c.env, scope, 10),
    topUpstreams(c.env, scope, 10),
    topUsers(c.env, scope, 10),
    recentErrors(c.env, scope),
    asyncJobStats(c.env, scope)
  ])

  const body: AdminUsageResponse = {
    range,
    dailyTotals: daily,
    topTools: tools,
    topUpstreams: upstreams,

    recentErrors: errors,
    asyncSummary: asyncStats.summary,

})

**Errors get their own menu item, both surfaces.** New nav entries **Errors** (`/app/errors`, self-scoped) and **Admin · Errors** (`/app/admin/errors`, with user attribution), each a focused page: range selector — sharing the sibling Usage dashboard's stored window, so flipping between the two keeps one consistent period — plus the existing ErrorsTable with its type/origin filters. Steven asked why remote token expiries aren't auto-refreshed. Flow mapped (2026-08-28):

**Refresh is strictly LAZY** — only in `resolveUserUpstreamBearer` (session init / reload_upstreams / admin Refresh-now). Fast path: access token >5min left used as-is (deliberate: eager refresh ROTATED single-use refresh tokens to death, June saga). Near-expiry → single-flight D1 lease (20s TTL). Static/Entra path: only `invalid_grant` flags needsReauth + skips future refreshes until reconnect; DCR/SDK path: ANY failure flags (SDK gives no transient signal + silently falls through to new-authz on unstructured errors), but self-heals at next session init if retry succeeds (saveTokens → clearReauthRequired). A6 gate blocks calls on flag, never refreshes. NO background refresh existed.

**Three death classes:** (1) idle expiry — provider inactivity window kills refresh token while unused (preventable by keep-warm); (2) rotation loss — refresh response never persisted → reuse-detection kills family; (3) grant invalidation — scope change/revocation (Datadog case 2026-08-27: audit `upstream.reauth_required` reason = RFC6749 invalid_grant boilerplate; Steven saw a SCOPE CHANGE consent on reconnect → class 3; §1a scrubber redacted the token Datadog echoed into its own error — scrub validated in the wild). Classes 2+3 un-preventable; keep-warm converts them to next-morning flags.

**Keep-warm BUILT (uncommitted at write time):** `upstream/keep-warm.ts` (`keepWarmUserCredentials`, injectable resolver for tests) + `listKeepWarmDueCredentials` in db/queries/upstream-credentials.ts + task 3 in the EXISTING nightly `0 3 * * *` cron (index.ts) — **no wrangler.toml / ops-template changes needed** (both crons already in all three configs). content.text:
Here's the full inventory and my proposal.

## What actually runs recurringly today

| Job | Trigger | Today's only trace | Worth listing? |
|---|---|---|---|
| git-sync due-check | hourly cron | `[cron]` log line (queued N/M) | ✅ |
| git-sync run (per repo) | queue, fed by due-check + manual | `git_sources.last_sync_status/error` — **latest run only, history overwritten** | ✅ the most valuable one |
| keep-warm refresh | nightly cron | log line (warmed X/Y) | ✅ |
| usage_events prune | nightly cron | log line | ✅ |
| async_jobs retention | nightly cron | log line | ✅ |
| oauth-client prune | nightly cron | log line + audit entry when >0 deleted | ✅ |
| cron heartbeat | every firing | KV key behind `/api/health` | not a job — it's the liveness signal, show as a banner |
| reindex consumer | queue, per doc save | none | ❌ too chatty — it's request-driven, not batch |
| usage ingest consumer | queue, per outbox drain | none | ❌ same |
| async `ctxlayer-jobs` runs | queue, per tool call | already has its own panel on Usage | ❌ covered |

The structural gap: **nothing keeps run history.** Console logs evaporate, `notify()` is fire-and-forget, and git-sync overwrites its status per repo. A dashboard needs a run ledger.

## Proposal

**1. Data: one `job_runs` table** (migration 0035): `id, task, started_at, duration_ms, status ('ok'|'error'|'skipped'), summary (JSON — task-specific counts like `{warmed: 3, due: 5}` or `{source: 'yuki-kb', imported: 2}`), error (scrubbed text, null)`. A tiny `recordJobRun(env, task, fn)` wrapper times the task, captures its returned summary or thrown error, writes the row — each cron task and the git-sync consumer get wrapped, ~2 lines each. Git-sync records one row **per repo run** (that's the granularity you debug at; hourly × few repos = bounded). Retention: the nightly prune task also deletes `job_runs` older than 90 days — and logs itself doing it.

**2. API:** `GET /api/admin/jobs?range=30d&task=git-sync` — same `parseRange`/`tz` machinery, plus a `task` filter param. Returns runs plus per-task aggregates (last run, success rate, avg duration).

**3. UI: Admin · Jobs**, between Usage and Audit in the nav. Same range selector (own stored scope), task filter select, and the graphical layer:

```
Admin · Jobs                                    [All types ▾] [Last 30d ▾]
⚠ banner only if the cron heartbeat is stale (scheduler itself dead)

┌ per-task strip timeline ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ git-sync        ●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●●✖●●●●●●●●●   97% · avg 4.2s     │
│ keep-warm       ·······●······●······✖·····    2/3 · avg 8.1s    │
│ usage-prune     ·······●······●······●·····    100%              │
│ oauth-prune     ·······●······●······●·····    100%              │
│ async-retention ·······●······●······●·····    100%              │
└──────── green dot = ok · red ✖ = error · hover = summary ─────────┘

Runs table: When · Task(badge) · Duration · Status · Summary(k=v preview)
  → row click opens drawer: full summary JSON + scrubbed error text
     (same pattern as the audit drawer)
```

The strip timeline is the "more graphical" centerpiece: one row per task, one mark per run positioned on the time axis, color = status — you see cadence gaps (a night the cron didn't fire shows as a hole) and error clusters at a glance, which neither a table nor the existing bar charts give you. Tiles above it for last-run/streak if we want more; the table below is the drill-down.

**Deliberately out:** reindex and usage consumers (request-driven noise, not batch jobs), async tool jobs (already on Usage). Both are one `recordJobRun` wrapper away if you ever change your mind.

**Bonus this unlocks for free:** git-sync finally gets *history* — today a failed nightly sync is overwritten by the next success, which is exactly the "error runs stamp last_synced_at" class of mystery you've hit before.

Rough size: migration + wrapper + 6 wrap sites, one endpoint + shared schema, one page with the timeline component (I'll load the dataviz skill for that) — comparable to yesterday's Errors work plus a chart. Anything you'd cut or add before I build — per-repo git-sync granularity and 90-day retention being the two defaults most worth challenging?

content: You're building a graphical Admin · Jobs dashboard showing cron/batch run history with range and task filters. I proposed the design (job_runs ledger, API, strip-timeline UI) and await your go-ahead or tweaks before building.

1	import { z } from 'zod'
2	import type { Env } from '../env'
3	import { runGitSync } from '../git/sync'
4	import { errMessage } from '../util/errors'
5	
6	/**
7	 * Batch consumer for ctxlayer-git-sync. One message per source per run.
8	 *
9	 * `runGitSync` records its own status on the source row and never throws
10	 * for ordinary sync failures (provider errors, no token) — those are
11	 * persisted as `last_sync_status='error'` and acked, since the next
12	 * scheduled/manual run retries. Only a truly unexpected throw retries
13	 * the message.
14	 */
15	const GitSyncMessage = z.object({
16	  sourceId: z.string().min(1),
17	  // Acting user for user_* read strategies (interactive "Sync now").
18	  userId: z.string().optional()
19	})
20	
21	export async function gitSyncConsumer(
22	  batch: MessageBatch,
23	  env: Env,
24	  _ctx: ExecutionContext
25	): Promise<void> {
26	  for (const msg of batch.messages) {
27	    const parsed = GitSyncMessage.safeParse(msg.body)
28	    if (!parsed.success) {
29	      console.error('git-sync-consumer: malformed message; dropping', { id: msg.id })
30	      msg.ack()
31	      continue
32	    }
33	    try {
34	      const result = await runGitSync(env, parsed.data.sourceId, { userId: parsed.data.userId })
35	      if (result.status === 'error') {
36	        console.warn('git-sync-consumer: sync recorded error', {
37	          sourceId: parsed.data.sourceId,
38	          error: result.error
39	        })
40	      }
41	      msg.ack()
42	    } catch (err) {
43	      console.error('git-sync-consumer: unexpected error; retrying', {
44	        id: msg.id,
45	        err: errMessage(err)
46	      })
47	      msg.retry()
48	    }
49	  }
50	}

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values — touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe — run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure — do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job — magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). → `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) — each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. → `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette — run the script, don't reason about ΔE.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,…>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory — or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, ≥8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. → `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer — by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. → `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For ≥ 2 series a legend is always present and ≤ 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box — the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** — its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout — open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** — it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue — it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale → two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake — see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light→dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD ΔE ≥ 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6–8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL — full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead — see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view — it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for ≥ 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** — values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance — every value filled in — is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical — steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of — build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong — check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** — every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

-- Run ledger for recurring batch jobs (cron tasks + git-sync runs),
-- powering Admin · Jobs. One row per run. Before this, cron outcomes
-- lived only in console logs (evaporate) and git-sync overwrote its
-- per-source status on every run — no history to debug from.
-- Rows are pruned after 90 days by the nightly 'jobs-prune' task.
CREATE TABLE job_runs (
  id          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  task        TEXT NOT NULL,
  started_at  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  duration_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('ok', 'partial', 'error')),
  summary     TEXT,  -- task-specific counts, JSON ({"warmed":3,"due":5})
  error       TEXT   -- scrubbed failure detail; NULL on ok
);
CREATE INDEX idx_job_runs_ts ON job_runs(started_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_job_runs_task_ts ON job_runs(task, started_at DESC);

content.text:
Probes settle it completely:

- `/api/health` → **302 to Access login** — roadmapper's health endpoint, the thing the bypass was *named* for, is blocked (so any external monitoring of it is broken too).
- `/api/admin/*` → reaches the worker unauthenticated (404 from the app itself, no Access in the way) — the bypass is real, and anyone on the internet gets straight through to roadmapper's admin API, protected only by whatever app-level auth roadmapper does or doesn't do.
- `/mcp` → 302 to Access login — so ctxlayer's `up-yuki-ia-nl` upstream does **not** ride this domain (it must point at a workers.dev or other host), meaning the bypass is *not* load-bearing for the gateway integration. Nothing breaks by fixing it.

**Diagnosis:** a copy-paste scoping mistake. Someone cloned the health-bypass pattern that `pdd` and `ctxlayer` use correctly and typed `/api/admin/*` where `/api/health` belonged — the policy name 'public health' on an admin path is the tell. Cloudflare's flag is fully warranted.

**The fix** (one API call, instantly reversible): retarget Access app `645d38dc` from `roadmapper.yukitools.dev/api/admin/*` to `roadmapper.yukitools.dev/api/health` and rename it 'roadmapper health (public)'. That simultaneously closes the admin-API hole and un-breaks the public health check, restoring the exact pattern its two siblings follow.

One caveat only you can rule out: if anything of yours deliberately calls roadmapper's `/api/admin/*` *without* an Access identity (an unauthenticated script or external automation), it would start getting 302s after the fix. Given the policy name, I'd bet against it — but roadmapper isn't a repo on this machine, so I can't verify its internals.

Say the word and I'll apply the retarget.

Done and noted for future Access work. Summary of the incident:

- **Root cause:** the `roadmapper api (public)` Access app carried a Bypass-everyone policy scoped to `/api/admin/*` — a copy-paste misscope of the per-host health-check pattern (its policy was even named 'public health'). Roadmapper's entire admin API was open at the Access layer, and its actual health endpoint was locked behind login.
- **Fix applied:** retargeted the app to `roadmapper.yukitools.dev/api/health`, matching the pdd/ctxlayer siblings. Verified live: health now 200 publicly, all `/api/admin/*` paths 302 to the Entra-gated login.
- **Side finding:** ctxlayer's `up-yuki-ia-nl` upstream doesn't ride that custom domain (its `/mcp` is Access-blocked), so nothing in the gateway was affected by either the hole or the fix.

I've saved the Access-app inventory and the root-Allow + health-Bypass pattern to memory, so future flags like this get checked against the intended shape before anyone touches a policy. The Cloudflare warning should clear on its next evaluation pass.

content.text:
Here's the precise risk picture, from the handler code and live probes — not the scanner's boilerplate.

## What the bypass actually exposes

**Scope, measured:** the bypass covers `/api/health` **and its subpaths** (`/api/health/sub` reaches the worker and 404s; `/api/healthx` and `/api/version` still 302 to Access login). So the exposed surface is exactly: whatever the worker routes under `/api/health/**`. Today that's one GET handler plus 404s — nothing else is mounted there.

**What an anonymous caller gets per request:**

1. **Disclosure, steady state:** deploy git SHA, build timestamp, and five dependency names with ok/latency. The SHA is the most substantive item: ctxlayer is a public MIT repo, so it maps to exact code — an attacker learns your patch level, deploy cadence, and uptime. Genuine recon value, but modest: the alternative (hiding versions of an open-source app) is thin obscurity.
2. **Disclosure, during outages — the one real leak:** `timed()`'s catch puts the raw dependency **error message** into the public payload (`error: errMessage(err)`). During a failure, anonymous callers see D1/KV/R2/Vectorize runtime error strings and cron staleness details ("stale: last cron 4000s ago"). No credentials — those never appear in binding errors — but it's internal diagnostic detail, publicly, precisely when you're weakest.
3. **Work amplification:** each anonymous hit executes ~5 backend operations (D1 `SELECT 1`, two KV gets, R2 head, Vectorize describe), unauthenticated and un-rate-limited app-side. A flooder burns request quota and micro-cents; Cloudflare's DDoS layer bounds it. Real but small.
4. **What it does *not* expose:** no route into the application — every other path stays Access-gated, and crucially ctxlayer has its own second wall: all `/api/*` handlers require the signed session cookie or admin role regardless of Access. Even deleting Access entirely wouldn't open data. The health endpoint itself is read-only probes; no mutation, no data read.

## So is the flag right?

The scanner is a heuristic that fires on *every* everyone-policy — it can't distinguish "accidentally public app" (roadmapper, real finding) from "intentionally public health check" (this, the pattern Cloudflare's own docs prescribe via Bypass). This one is working-as-designed; the finding is archivable in Security Center as accepted risk, which is the honest disposition.

## If you want to tighten anyway, in value order

1. **Drop the `error` string from the public payload** — keep name/ok/latency (a monitor needs "which dep is down", not the raw message; the full text stays in logs). Kills the only real information leak, one small code change. This one I'd actually do.
2. **A WAF rate rule on the exact path** — kills the amplification nit for free.
3. **IP-scope the bypass** to your monitor's egress IPs — removes "everyone" and the flag itself, but breaks casual curl checks (including my post-deploy verification) from arbitrary networks.
4. Also worth one code comment in `health.ts`: *nothing may ever be mounted under `/api/health/**`* — the subpath-inclusive bypass makes that an invariant someone could silently break in two years.

Say the word on 1 (+4) and I'll make the change; 2 and 3 are dashboard config if you want them.

content: Reviewing the Cloudflare flag on ctxlayer's public health endpoint: it's an intentional bypass, safe to accept, but the payload leaks raw dependency error text during outages. Next action: your go-ahead to strip that error field and add a guard comment.

 *

 *      binding errors during an outage are internal diagnostics, not
 *      something to hand every visitor exactly when we're weakest.
 */
export const healthRoute = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env }>()

content.text:
That's the in-app AI drafting flow from the July skills overhaul — ctxlayer hands your agent the context, your agent writes the skill, ctxlayer persists it. No server-side LLM anywhere.

**How it works:**

1. **Two equivalent entry points:** the `/draft-skill` MCP prompt (shows in Claude Code's slash list — args: `upstreams` as comma-separated slugs, optional `intent` and `tool`) and the `draft_skill` tool (same content, for clients that don't render prompts — Desktop). Example: `/ctxlayer:draft-skill upstreams=up-linear intent="how we file and triage issues"`.
2. **ctxlayer returns a context bundle**, not a draft: the upstream's full tool catalogue (native names + schemas), an optional focus tool, related org docs, one or two published skills as house-style references, your intent, plus the drafter guidance — lead with the scenario, numbered concrete steps, reference tools by **native** names in backticks (never the mangled `slug__tool` form — that hardcodes the install), multi-upstream requests get one woven workflow, keep it under ~500 lines.
3. **The agent drafts, then calls `save_draft_skill`** — never prints the skill as its answer. That saves a **private draft owned by you** (any signed-in user can author, not just admins). Passing a `skillId` or an existing own slug instead **upserts a new revision** of that skill — history preserved, and if it's already published the edit goes live to the org. A linter runs after save (warning-only — it's what catches mangled tool references), and the markdown body is converted to editor blocks server-side — including pipe tables since last week's fix.
4. **Publish and attach from `/app/skills`:** publishing makes it org-visible (feeds `list_skills`, the prompts picker, the instructions guidance block, the first-result hint); attaching it to an upstream or a specific tool is the admin step that lights up the discovery channels.

Worth remembering why it exists in its current shape: it's also the security worked-example in CLAUDE.md — the bundle inlines upstream descriptions next to first-party guidance, so everything passes the sanitisation gate, and it resolves upstreams through the visibility + per-tool ACL path so a non-admin can't use it as a read oracle for ungranted upstreams.

And the standing reason to reach for it: your Desktop diagnostic's coverage gap — 231 tools on linear (60), github (44), ado (42) and friends with **zero** attached skills. `draft_skill` is exactly the authoring path meant to close that backlog, one playbook at a time.

ctxlayer — the gateway your org calls "Yuki MCP" — is your org's curated context layer. Upstream tools are proxied as `<upstream-slug>__<tool>`; alongside them:

- `list_upstreams` — your visible upstreams, each with its `attached_skills` / `attached_docs` (the org playbooks for that service).

A SKILL is a short, declarative playbook the agent reads to understand *this org's conventions* for a given tool. It is NOT a generic tool reference (the schema is already visible to the agent).

The JSON context bundle below has these sections:
  upstreams      — ONE OR MORE MCP upstreams. Each has: name + slug + transport, an `allTools` catalogue, an optional `focusTool` (schema for a specific tool), and usage.
  relatedDocs    — org docs related to the upstream(s), if any
  styleSkills    — 1-2 existing published skills as house-style refs
  operatorPrompt — freeform request from the operator (if any)

Body guidance:
- Lead with a short paragraph naming the scenario and the outcome.
- Then a numbered list of concrete steps (call tool X with these args, then tool Y with these args).
- Reference attached tools by their `name` field from the bundle (the native upstream tool name) in backticks — e.g. `wit_work_item`, `repo_file` — and name the owning upstream once in prose (e.g. "via the ADO upstream"). Do NOT use the `mangledName` / `<slug>__tool` form: it hardcodes this install's slug into the body and breaks the skill if the upstream is re-registered or reused on another install. The agent resolves the native name to the callable form at run time.
- When the bundle has MORE THAN ONE upstream, design a SINGLE cohesive workflow that weaves their tools together — not two parallel sections. Name each upstream in prose so the agent knows which server a tool belongs to.

## Step 2: Gather Codebase Context

### CRITICAL: Use `request_task_context` + `poll_task_context` — Not Native Agents

Driver MCP's request/poll pair is your primary workflow. **It is your default for codebase context.**

**What the workflow does:** `request_task_context` spawns a specialized context agent on Driver's servers that reads pre-computed, exhaustive codebase documentation — architecture overviews, code maps, file-level documentation, changelogs — and does live runtime analysis. `poll_task_context` retrieves its status and, when complete, the synthesized task-specific dynamic context: relevant architecture, key files, conventions, and suggested approaches.

**How to use it:** Call `request_task_context` with a detailed task description and verified codebase names. It immediately returns a `request_id`; it does not return the context directly. ```text

**The context agent takes on the order of several minutes. This is expected and normal.** First poll after roughly 30-45 seconds, then every 20-30 seconds. A `QUEUED` or `RUNNING` status means it is still working; keep doing useful work and poll again. A `COMPLETED` status includes the synthesized context. If the status is `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`, report the returned error instead of polling indefinitely. If it is still pending well past roughly 10 minutes, treat it as stalled: report it and resubmit rather than polling forever.

### CRITICAL: Do NOT Substitute Native Agents
